lesson_title: A Bathtub a Day: How Your Kidneys Filter Everything and Take It Back
hook_text: Your kidneys filter 180 litres a day, more than a full bathtub, and you only pee out one and a half. Where does the rest go?
clip_script: Every cell makes rubbish just by living. Burn glucose for energy and the smoke is carbon dioxide. Break down extra protein in the liver and the ash is urea. Let them pile up and your cells are poisoned. Getting rid of rubbish your cells made is excretion. Not faeces, that is egestion, leftovers that never got into your body. Three exits: lungs breathe out the carbon dioxide, skin sweats out water and salt, and the kidneys handle the urea. How? With a sieve. Blood is squeezed through tiny vessels and everything small falls through: water, glucose, salt, urea. Blood cells and proteins stay. That is 180 litres a day, a whole bathtub. Then the kidney goes back through the pile and takes back the treasure: every bit of glucose, 99 drops of water in every 100, the salt you need. The urea stays. What drips out, one and a half litres, is urine. Hot day, lots of sweat? The kidney takes back more water and your urine goes dark. Pale means hydrated. Dark means drink. Keep the sieves flushed and they will last a lifetime.
visual_style: A bathtub fills with 180 litres then pours through a glowing sieve; coins, pens and sweets fall through and most jump back into a bag, leaving a small cup of yellow liquid; a urine colour strip slides from pale to dark under a sun.
pacing: Fast setup on rubbish, a measured two-step on filter then reclaim, a quick colour-strip finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain filtration and reabsorption in three sentences.
